note: Regional context compiled from Namibian Government statements as reported in the media, the European Union delegation in Namibia and South African and Namibian media. These figures are not South African programme data and never feed the headline figures on the other tabs. Where reports differ, we show each figure with its source.
summary: On 23 September 2026 Namibia confirmed foot and mouth disease on a commercial farm in the Karasburg state veterinary district of the ||Kharas region, inside its WOAH-recognised zone free without vaccination and its first outbreak in that zone in about 60 years. By 14 October the SAT1 outbreak had reached 18 farms, with 131 animals positive out of 63,011 inspected (unchanged on 20 October, when the chief veterinary officer confirmed it remained confined to the Karasburg district), and compulsory vaccination in three rounds over three months began that day. A second outbreak was confirmed on Kalala Island in the Zambezi region in early October; officials say it has no epidemiological link to ||Kharas, and 42,286 cattle there had been vaccinated by 21 October, when 1,296 cattle on 25 Karasburg farms had also been vaccinated. Namibia has suspended exports of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products, the European Union and the United States have restricted imports, and live exports of weaners and slaughter sheep to South Africa have stopped. Roadblocks around Karasburg could stay until 23 December, and industry bodies on both sides are setting out positions on the protocols that would let trade with South Africa resume. Namibia's mid-year budget proposes N$179 million for containment, and our feedlot association has said it will not support cattle and beef imports from Namibia and Botswana for now. On 26 October officials confirmed the whole ||Kharas region is a control area, to be split into smaller containment zones, while farmers there warn of job losses. By 27 October more than 50,000 cattle had been vaccinated in Zambezi, where more than 1,300 cattle are reported affected, and Meatco ran a two-day slaughter of its own feedlot cattle for the domestic market only. On 28 October the ministry reported no new cases in either region and more than 61,000 cattle vaccinated: 7,402 on 81 farms in ||Kharas and 53,913 in Zambezi.

kpis.sub: Proposed in Namibia's mid-year budget review, reported 23 October 2026. The agriculture ministry had estimated N$190 million on 4 October, including a 290 kilometre control fence costed at about N$47 million. No compensation scheme for farmers was announced.

regions.name: ||Kharas region, Karasburg state veterinary district
regions.status: 18 farms infected and 131 animals positive of 63,011 inspected, as at 14 October, unchanged at 15 October (Notification No. 20). The first surveillance round covered 82 farms within 30 kilometres of the index farm; the second round, extended to 50 kilometres, had inspected 11 of 65 targeted farms. Compulsory vaccination by state veterinary officials began on 14 October under Veterinary Public Notification No. 19 of 2026: three rounds over three months, ending in mid-January 2027, covering all farms south of the B3 and C10 roads to the Orange River. Owners may not vaccinate their own animals. Eighteen roadblocks operate in ||Kharas, Khomas and Otjozondjupa. By 21 October, 1,296 cattle on 25 farms had been vaccinated, of about 13,000 targeted in the first round (New Era, 22 October, which dates the start to 17 October). On 26 October veterinary officials confirmed the whole ||Kharas region is a control area (all movement of live cloven-hoofed animals into, out of and within it suspended) and said it will be split into smaller containment zones using game fences (The Namibian, 26 October). By 28 October, 7,402 cattle on 81 farms had been vaccinated, no new cases had been found, and the second surveillance round had inspected and sampled 10 farms (New Era, 29 October).
regions.border: Borders our Northern Cape along the Orange River.

regions.name: Zambezi region, Kalala Island (Kabbe constituency)
regions.status: 12 positive samples; no new clinical cases by 13 October after six teams examined 6,226 cattle at 17 crush pens. 10,864 cattle vaccinated by 13 October (2,942 at Kalala, then 7,922 at 11 crush pens), rising to 42,286 at 34 crush pens by 21 October, with no new cases outside the disease management area. Roadblocks at Luhonono and Nakabolelwa are staffed jointly with the police. Five roadblocks from 14 October (Kongola, Selela, Luhonono, Bukalo, Nakabolelwa). Officials report no epidemiological link to ||Kharas. New Era dates confirmation to 6 October; earlier reports said 7 October. Auctions, movement and slaughter remain suspended, and The Namibian reports lost income for local meat sellers and households (18 October). By 27 October more than 50,000 cattle had been vaccinated over two weeks, and New Era reported more than 1,300 cattle affected at 18 crush pens, with infection spread across Kabbe South, Kabbe North, Katima Rural and Kongola, nearly three-quarters of the district. Checkpoint staff at Nakabolelwa and Luhonono reported staff and supply shortages (minister's visit, New Era, 27 October). On 28 October the ministry reported no new cases, about 1,300 cases at 18 crush pens confined to Kalala Island, and 53,913 cattle vaccinated at 37 crush pens (New Era, 29 October).
regions.border: Namibia's north-eastern vaccination zone; does not border South Africa.

progression.detail: Index farm, Karasburg. 63 cattle showed clinical signs.
Surveillance from 22 to 25 September across five regions; all positives in the Karasburg district.
Affected farms up from three to five.
15,096 animals inspected on 66 of 81 targeted farms. SAT1 confirmed.

29,313 animals inspected on 68 farms. The Namibian reports 127 cattle with clinical signs from laboratory testing of 2,910 cattle, 22,289 sheep, 4,114 goats and 9 pigs, plus clinical signs in 50 sheep, 1 goat and 1 pig.
72 of 81 farms within 50 kilometres inspected; 2,292 vehicles searched at seven checkpoints.
63,011 animals inspected. Second surveillance round (50 kilometres) at 11 of 65 farms. Counted as animals testing positive, not samples.
Unchanged from 14 October; outbreak still confined to the Karasburg district (Veterinary Public Notification No. 20 of 2026). Counted as animals testing positive.
Unchanged since 14 October, per the chief veterinary officer; movement controls in the Karasburg veterinary district to be tightened. Reported as cases.
Zambezi region, not ||Kharas: more than 1,300 cattle affected at 18 crush pens, across four constituencies. Counted as cattle affected, not laboratory positives. No new ||Kharas count reported.
||Kharas unchanged; no new cases in ||Kharas or Zambezi (Zambezi about 1,300 cases at 18 crush pens on Kalala Island; the report does not say whether these are cases or animals). Reported as cases.

timeline.event: Samples taken from 11 cattle with clinical signs on a commercial farm near Karasburg. WOAH suspends the free zone's status with effect from this date.
timeline.source: African Farming; EU delegation to Namibia

timeline.event: Outbreak confirmed. Veterinary Public Notification No. 15 of 2026 activates the national contingency plan and suspends movement, slaughter, imports and exports of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products nationwide.
Namibia notifies WOAH. Meatco suspends beef exports and slaughter and reconciles consignments already in transit.
Sixteen veterinary checkpoints begin operating to stop unauthorised movement of livestock and meat.
Movement restored north of the veterinary cordon fence and allowed under strict conditions south of it, except in the ||Kharas region.
The United States issues an import alert for all of Namibia, effective 23 September, covering live ruminants, swine and their germplasm.
The Ministry of Agriculture estimates containment will cost about N$190 million, including a 290 kilometre control fence, vaccination and targeted culling.
The European Union publishes a temporary suspension of fresh meat imports from the previously free zone.
Namibian and South African technical officials meet online on protocols to reopen livestock auctions; South African animal health experts due in Namibia on 9 October.

Farmer's Weekly reports that Cabinet has approved a containment plan with a buffer zone, ring vaccination and veterinary cordon fencing along the border with South Africa. The same day, a second outbreak is confirmed in the Zambezi region.
Agriculture minister Inge Zaamwani tells Parliament that culling is no longer viable and vaccination is the only option, with 100,000 doses available.

Namibian farmers' bodies hold an informal exchange with a South African delegation (RPO, AgriSA and RMIS) on protocols, permits and traceability for moving animals from restricted areas to abattoirs. No agreements were reached; Namibian industry is to prepare an evidence-based proposal for both countries' veterinary authorities.
Construction starts on a veterinary cordon fence along the Orange River from Homerevier to Velloorsdrift, expected to take four months.
Agriculture minister Inge Zaamwani ends a two-day visit to the Karasburg district, checking roadblocks and fence work; vaccination teams are assembling at a camp in Karasburg.
The Directorate of Veterinary Services says construction of the containment zone fence starts this week, alongside the Orange River cordon fence already under way.
Meatco confirms about 400 production workers are on three weeks of paid special leave (1 to 23 October) while exports are suspended; it will review the position on 23 October.

Compulsory vaccination begins in the Karasburg state veterinary district under Veterinary Public Notification No. 19 of 2026, in three rounds over three months. Five strategic roadblocks start in the Zambezi region.
Meatco proposes two-thirds pay for staff from November 2026 to January 2027 and a voluntary separation programme, after revenue fell by N$757 million in 2025/26.

Police and the Karasburg state veterinary office tighten fixed and occasional roadblocks around the 17 farms near the index farm, including Warmbad and Velloorsdrift; the police say the operation could run until 23 December.

Veterinary Public Notification No. 20 of 2026 confirms the outbreak is still confined to the Karasburg district. Movement north of the cordon fence stays permitted except in the Zambezi region; feedlot and quarantine animals may go to registered abattoirs after 30 days without new intake and negative tests.
The Economic Association of Namibia warns the outbreak threatens the expected livestock recovery; it cites 63,011 animals inspected in the Karasburg district as at 14 October.

The chief veterinary officer confirms 131 cases on 18 farms, unchanged since 14 October, and says surveillance and movement controls in the Karasburg district will be stepped up. The Namibia Chamber of Commerce and Industry gives N$1.5 million to the FMD support fund.
The agriculture ministry's weekly update reports 1,296 cattle vaccinated on 25 farms in Karasburg and 42,286 in the Zambezi region, with no new cases outside the Zambezi disease management area.
Namibia's mid-year budget review proposes N$179 million to contain foot and mouth disease; no compensation scheme for farmers is announced.
Four men, including a farmer, are arrested for allegedly transporting raw meat in breach of the movement regulations.

Veterinary officials in Keetmanshoop confirm the whole ||Kharas region is a control area, with all movement of live cloven-hoofed animals into, out of and within it suspended; the region is to be split into smaller containment zones using game fences. Farmers warn of job losses and ask for supervised movement from unaffected farms.
Agriculture Minister Inge Zaamwani visits the Zambezi region; more than 50,000 cattle have been vaccinated there over two weeks and more than 1,300 cattle are reported affected at 18 crush pens.
Meatco begins a two-day temporary slaughter (27 and 28 October) of cattle already in its feedlots, with all beef for the domestic market; normal slaughter has been suspended since 23 September.

The ministry reports no new cases in either region; more than 61,000 cattle vaccinated (7,402 in ||Kharas, 53,913 in Zambezi). Eighteen roadblocks operate across ||Kharas, Hardap, Khomas and Otjozondjupa, and exports of animals from outside ||Kharas may proceed subject to destination requirements.

trade.measure: Temporary suspension of fresh meat of cattle, sheep, goats and other ungulates, and of biltong and jerky-type products, from the previously free zone.
trade.detail: Meat given the most severe risk-reducing treatment may still enter. Fresh meat certified before 23 September may enter within 90 days of that date. Trade preferences under the EU-SADC agreement are unchanged. The EU takes more than 80 percent of Namibia's beef exports.
trade.source: EU delegation to Namibia; Maroela Media

trade.measure: Import alert for the whole country on live ruminants, camelids, swine and their germplasm, with extra conditions on animal products.
Namibian exports of live cloven-hoofed animals, including weaner calves and slaughter sheep, have stopped. Auction trade is under discussion.
trade.detail: South Africa had received 36,821 weaner calves and 417,808 slaughter sheep from Namibia so far in 2026. Namibian sheep make up about 15 percent of our slaughter supply, so the RPO expects a larger price effect on mutton and lamb than on beef.

trade.measure: Export and local abattoir slaughter suspended in the affected areas; Meatco operations halted.
trade.detail: Butcheries in ||Kharas report putting staff on leave. Modelling cited by The Namibian suggests about 12,000 jobs could be lost in 2026 and 2027, and no exemption from the agricultural minimum wage is being considered.

sa_links.detail: The ||Kharas outbreak lies along the Orange River border with our Northern Cape. Namibia is fencing that border and investigating the source along the river. Namibian officials had warned earlier of unregistered livestock crossing from South Africa.

Minister Aucamp said South Africa has made 50,000 vaccine doses available to Namibia, Eswatini and Lesotho this year, and that resuming red meat imports from Namibia and Botswana depends on agreed biosecurity protocols.

The loss of Namibian weaners and slaughter sheep tightens our supply, with mutton and lamb most exposed. The RPO reports weaner calf prices of about R57 to R60 a kilogram and a jump of nearly R9 a kilogram in A2 lamb carcass prices within a week, and warns that some abattoirs could close; it questions whether the rises reflect a real shortage.
sa_links.source: Farmer's Weekly, 6 October 2026; The Namibian, 14 October 2026

sa_links.detail: Technical officials of both countries are working on conditions to reopen auctions once the Karasburg outbreak is shown to be contained. At an informal exchange on 9 October, a South African delegation from the RPO, AgriSA and RMIS shared our experience of permits and traceability for moving animals to abattoirs. No agreements were reached; only the two governments can negotiate market access, and formal approval could take six to seven months.
sa_links.source: The Namibian, 6 October 2026; New Era, 14 October 2026

sa_links.detail: RMIS wants separate protocols for sheep and cattle. Imported sheep must be free of FMD risk, and cattle would need to come from below the ||Kharas red zone, be vaccinated and spend at least two weeks in a feedlot, meeting the same standards as our own herds. RMIS also asks for reciprocity on South African genetic material. Final protocols rest with the two veterinary authorities. Between 80 and 90 percent of Namibian sheep are destined for our market. On 20 October the South African Feedlot Association said it will not support imports of live cattle and beef from Namibia and Botswana while the disease remains a concern, despite a local calf shortage, and will review this later.
sa_links.source: Food For Mzansi, 20 October 2026; The Namibian, 21 October 2026

sa_links.detail: Namibia's Livestock and Livestock Products Board reports that, before the outbreak halted movements, South Africa took 46.9 percent of Namibian lamb and mutton exports by volume this year and 78,746 live goats went to our feedlots. South Africa also supplied 30.9 percent of Namibia's pork imports. The board expects a weaker final quarter.

open_questions: Serotype of the Zambezi outbreak; a 29 October New Era report refers to serotype O and SAT, but no official notification has confirmed it. Officials report no epidemiological link to ||Kharas.
Whether Namibia will subdivide its former free zone so that unaffected areas can resume exports; officials have said a plan could take about six months to reach WOAH.

Whether the veterinary authorities of Namibia and South Africa accept an industry proposal for supervised movement of animals from unaffected areas to abattoirs; on 26 October Namibian officials could not say when bio-secure transit routes might be approved.
